title: Epidemiology and Subtype Distribution of Respiratory Syncytial Virus in Children Aged 0-36 Months With Severe Acute Respiratory Infection in Mato Grosso do Sul, a Brazilian Border State, 2022-2024.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) in children. We describe RSV-associated SARI in children up to 36 months, including seasonality, A/B subtyping, and clinical profile, in Mato Grosso do Sul, a Brazilian border state.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective, surveillance-based descriptive study used SIVEP-Gripe data on RSV-positive SARI cases notified in 2022-2024. A convenience subset of preserved samples with Ct ≤ 27 (313 typed; 13.9% of cases) underwent duplex RT-qPCR typing. Typed samples were a non-random subset, and clinical data had missing values.
analysis.methods: Seasonality was assessed with quasi-Poisson regression; clinical features were compared using chi-square or Fisher's exact tests and Wilcoxon tests.
analysis.main_results: Among 9758 SARI cases, 2254 (23%) were RSV positive. Peak activity was highest in 2023 (Week 14). Most cases (75%) occurred in infants younger than 12 months. Among cases with information, 79.5% (1502/1889) received ventilatory support (8.4% invasive), 14.2% (294/2076) required ICU admission, and 37 died (case fatality 1.6%). From July 2023, with all samples tested for rhinovirus, adenovirus, and human metapneumovirus, 18.4% of cases had codetection, mostly rhinovirus. Among typed samples, RSV-B accounted for 31/37 in 2022 and 104/137 in 2024, and RSV-A accounted for 131/138 in 2023. Deaths among typed cases (6/170 RSV-A and 0/142 RSV-B) all occurred in 2023.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: RSV was a frequent cause of SARI hospitalization in this Brazilian border state, mainly among infants. RSV-A and RSV-B cocirculated with comparable clinical profiles; subtype-specific mortality could not be assessed because all deaths among typed cases occurred in 2023.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the need for targeted surveillance and intervention strategies for RSV in young children, particularly infants, in Brazilian border states. They also highlight the importance of considering co-infections with other respiratory viruses in clinical management.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is moderate due to the limitations in sample selection and data completeness.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the epidemiology and subtype distribution of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in children aged 0-36 months with severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) in Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil, from 2022 to 2024. RSV was found to be a significant cause of SARI hospitalization, particularly among infants. The study reports that 23% of SARI cases were RSV positive, with peak activity in 2023. RSV-A and RSV-B cocirculated, but subtype-specific mortality could not be determined due to all deaths occurring in 2023. The study highlights the importance of RSV surveillance in this region and the need for further research on its clinical impact. However, the evidence is moderate due to the non-random sample selection and missing clinical data.

title: Pathogens associated with childhood febrile illness in West Africa: a systematic review

analysis.research_question_and_background: Background Up to 80% of children seeking medical attention in Africa present with acute febrile illness.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This systematic review has been registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under the registration number: CRD 42023466517.
analysis.methods: A literature search was conducted in Medline and Embase via OVID, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Connecting Repositories (CoRE), Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), African Journals Online (AJOL) and World Health Organisation (WHO) Africa Index Medicus, for studies published from 2013 to 2023.
analysis.main_results: Results We included 84 studies from 11 West African countries.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings reveal important gaps in the existing evidence base for febrile pathogen detection and highlight areas where future primary research with a broader diagnostic scope would provide more complete epidemiological data.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Epidemiological data on the locally circulating pathogens causing fever are essential to inform clinical management and for public health interventions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Only 8% of studies performed comprehensive investigations (concurrent testing across ≥ 3 pathogen classes in the same participant) for a wide range of pathogens.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review aimed to understand the aetiologies of febrile illness among children in West Africa. It included 84 studies from 11 countries, highlighting that diagnostic testing was predominantly blood-based, with limited investigation of gastrointestinal, zoonotic, and emerging pathogens. Human metapneumovirus was identified as a significant pathogen, with findings indicating the need for broader diagnostic approaches. The study underscores the importance of comprehensive pathogen detection for improved clinical management and public health interventions. However, the limited number of studies that tested across multiple pathogen classes suggests a gap in the current evidence base. The evidence strength is moderate due to the variability in diagnostic methods and the focus on blood-based testing.

title: Generative AI-Driven Hybrid Optimized Deep Learning Model for Computational Intelligence Predicting HMPV Virus Infections in Healthcare

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the challenges in diagnosing HMPV infections due to their nonspecific clinical presentation and lack of routine testing, thereby improving patient outcomes and optimizing healthcare interventions.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study employed a hybrid deep learning model integrating GANs, CNN-RNN, and QSVM to predict HMPV infections, validated across three hospital networks.
analysis.methods: The model utilized GAN-based synthetic data augmentation, hybrid CNN-RNN for feature extraction, and QSVM for classification, all validated across various hospital networks and patient populations.
analysis.main_results: The model achieved 96.2% accuracy, 96.1% F1-score, and 0.983 AUC-ROC, with 5%–7% higher performance and 32% fewer false negatives compared to traditional approaches.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The model's innovations, including GAN-based data augmentation, hybrid CNN-RNN, and QSVM optimization, resolved key issues in medical AI, enhancing interpretability and real-time processing.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The model's high accuracy and real-time capabilities significantly improve early detection and treatment of HMPV infections, benefiting high-risk groups like young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised patients.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The model's robustness and generalizability were ensured through rigorous cross-validation across various hospital networks and patient populations, but limitations include the need for large, diverse datasets.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduced an AI-based hybrid deep learning model for predicting HMPV infections, achieving high accuracy and real-time processing, which significantly improves early detection and treatment of HMPV infections in high-risk groups.
